findings.title: A DAS contract description states business meaning, duplicating the DAB definition it must defer to
findings.detail:
The `unit_price` column description runs: "Edm.Decimal with Scale=Variable, Nullable=false. The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it. **This is the price on the line, which is not necessarily the product's current price.**" (lines 46-49). The first two sentences are system vocabulary and correct. The third is business meaning, and it is a second copy of what `dab/model.yaml:151-152` already says about `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE`: "What was agreed when the order was accepted, which is not what the goods cost today and does not move when the price does." It also speaks in DAB's word rather than the source's -- the source calls the row an `OrderDetails`, not a "line"; `ORDER_LINE` is the entity this slice invented in `dab/model.yaml:121`.

`docs/conventions.md` §1.1 is a hard rule: "A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. Never what it means to the business," with the why "Business meaning has exactly one home (§1.2)." §1.2 repeats it from the other side: an entity's `definition` "is the **only** place the data is explained... Two definitions eventually mean two numbers." The contract's own header comment, lines 3-4, restates the rule it then breaks: "Descriptions stay in the source's vocabulary -- what a thing MEANS is dab/model.yaml's job, and saying it twice is how two numbers start disagreeing."

This is the only such sentence in the repository. Every other description across all three contracts is strictly `Edm.<type>`, nullability, a referential constraint, or a note about the service's own spelling -- including the closest analogue, `das/contracts/orders.yaml:73-74` for `freight`, which stops at "The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it" and says nothing about what freight is. It is not registered in `docs/deviations.md`, and none of the four ADRs this slice landed (0009-0012) mention it; ADR 0011, which decided the `Discount` type, is the one that touched this file and it did not touch this line.
findings.why_it_matters: DAS's whole job is to say what the source said and interpret nothing, so an interpretation here is the layer failing at the one thing it exists for -- and it is the direction the layering rules are weakest against, because nothing mechanical checks it (no test in `tests/` scans contract descriptions; ruff, ty, sqlfluff and yamllint cannot see prose). Concretely, `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE` in `dab/model.yaml` carries one qualification the DAS copy does not: "It is the price before any discount." A reader who trusts the contract already has an incomplete definition, and slice 5 lands the `Products` contract with its own `UnitPrice` -- the moment somebody sharpens the DAB definition against that new entity, the DAS sentence becomes the stale second definition, in the layer that is furthest from the model and is read by anyone auditing what the source actually sent. `docs/conventions.md` §11 names the cheap fixes: delete the sentence (the DAB description already carries it), or, if the point is genuinely structural, say it structurally as `orders.yaml:35-36` does -- "Referential constraint to Products.ProductId" -- which is a fact about the source rather than about the business.

result.summary: No data-flow crossing in this slice. DAR reads only `dab.*` (`dar/uss/order_line.sql`, the `ordered*` CTEs in `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`); the destination reads only `dar__uss`, via the question's own `uss.sql`, and adds no query of its own; `docs/questions/04-revenue-per-order-month/staged.sql` reads only `das__staged.*__current`, with `dab`/`dar__uss` appearing solely in a stripped comment as in questions 1-3; the new mapping keeps source words to the permitted keys; `checks/order_line_is_part_of_order__resolves.sql` reading `dar__uss` copies the slice-2 precedent exactly. No business word appears under `src/` and no source name appears as an id or name in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` (`QUANTITY` is the example `docs/conventions.md` §1.2 itself blesses). One leak in the opposite direction: the new DAS contract's `unit_price` description explains what the value means to the business and restates the DAB definition of `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE`, against a hard rule that the same file's header comment quotes.

findings.title: A DAS contract description carries business meaning, restating dab/model.yaml's definition
findings.detail:
The `unit_price` column's description reads: "Edm.Decimal with Scale=Variable, Nullable=false. The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it. **This is the price on the line, which is not necessarily the product's current price.**" (lines 46-49).

That last sentence is business meaning, and it is a second copy of a definition that already exists: `dab/model.yaml:149-152` defines `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE` as "The price per unit the business agreed to on this line" with the description "What was agreed when the order was accepted, which is not what the goods cost today and does not move when the price does."

This breaks two hard rules:
- §1.1: "A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. **Never what it means to the business.**"
- §1.2: "Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` in business language, and that is the **only** place the data is explained."

The file's own header comment (lines 3-4) states the rule it breaks: "Descriptions stay in the source's vocabulary -- what a thing MEANS is dab/model.yaml's job, and saying it twice is how two numbers start disagreeing."

Every other column in this repository's three contracts obeys it — `orders.yaml` and `customers.yaml` carry only Edm types, nullability, referential constraints and spelling notes; `order_details.yaml`'s own `freight`-equivalent line 47 ("The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it") is fine because it is about the recording. Only this one sentence crosses over. The fix is to delete it; `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE` already says it.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the exact drift §1.1 and §1.2 exist to prevent: the meaning of the price now lives in two files, and the day the model's definition is refined the contract will be the stale copy nobody regenerates. It is also precedent — the next contract author reads this file as the pattern.

findings.title: ADR 0012 records a change to ADR 0002 that was not made and, under the ADR rules, cannot be
findings.detail:
ADR 0012's Decision Outcome states: "The property is proved for measures, **the limit of that proof is written into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule**, and a question whose answer query aggregates a peripheral's numeric column is refused by the question checker."

It was not written into ADR 0002. `docs/adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md:112` still reads "**Two** rules follow from the contract and are written down because they are query-time traps" and still lists exactly two (INNER vs LEFT on an inherited key; a ratio is `sum(a)/sum(b)`). The only edit this slice made to ADR 0002 was inside its Confirmation section (lines 160-165).

And it could not have been written there. `docs/adr/README.md:3-4` — "A record is **superseded by a new file, never edited**" — with exactly one exception, README:8-11, the Confirmation section. Line 112 is in the decision body, so amending it is forbidden; superseding ADR 0002 was not done either.

ADR 0012's own Consequences section contradicts its Decision Outcome on the same point: line 79 says "ADR 0002 already publishes two query-time rules and neither covers this one; a third would be true, unread and unenforced."

The result is that the bridge's published contract — the thing ADR 0002 says "every consumer is written against" — is silent about a rule every consumer must now obey. `.claude/skills/dar/SKILL.md:52` already announces "Three consequences at query time" against ADR 0002's two.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader who follows ADR 0012 to ADR 0002 to find the third rule will not find it, and a reader of ADR 0002 alone will believe the contract is complete. The fix that the record implies is the one the ADR rules forbid, so the decision as written cannot be carried out — it needs a different home (see the conventions.md §10 finding) or a superseding record.

findings.title: A new hard rule on questions is documented in two skill files but not in the one convention document
findings.detail:
This slice introduces a new hard rule that every question in the repository must satisfy: an answer query may apply an aggregate only to `_measure__` columns, and `count(*)` over the bridge is refused. It is enforced by `src/adss/question.py:_refuse_an_aggregate_the_bridge_does_not_protect` and run against every question.

conventions.md §10 (the Questions table, lines 234-241) was not touched. The rule is instead stated in prose in two other places added by this slice:
- `.claude/skills/adss/SKILL.md:96` — "An answer query may aggregate `_measure__` columns and nothing else, and it is refused if it does otherwise."
- `.claude/skills/dar/SKILL.md:59` — "**Aggregate `_measure__` columns and nothing else.** A question's `uss.sql` is refused if it applies any aggregate to a peripheral's column, or writes `count(*)` over the bridge..."

conventions.md's preamble is explicit about where this belongs: "The **one** convention document... There is deliberately no second machine-readable copy of these rules. Where an **off-the-shelf** tool can already check a rule, the tool's configuration is the rule and this page records only the reason." `src/adss/question.py` is this repository's own machinery, not an off-the-shelf tool, so the exemption does not apply — and §10's existing rows are precisely the pattern for machinery-enforced question rules ("Both halves are checked", "and the machinery proves it").

The skills' own convention is to point at conventions.md for rules — `.claude/skills/dab/SKILL.md:41` says of M1-M7, "They are in `docs/conventions.md` §1.4". The two new skill paragraphs point at ADR 0012 instead, because there is nothing in conventions.md to point at.
findings.why_it_matters: This is a second copy with no first copy, which is the drift the preamble names: "the two copies disagree within a quarter, and the disagreement is discovered by an argument in a pull request." A reviewer checking a question against §10 will not know the rule exists, and the two skill statements already differ in scope — only the dar one mentions `count(*)`.

findings.title: A generated check emits an unaliased table reference, the only one in the repository
findings.detail:
Line 7 is `    FROM das__staged.order_details__current` — no alias. conventions.md §3: "Every table reference has an explicit alias, and a join condition names the earlier table first." §3's preamble states all of its rules are hard rules.

sqlfluff does not catch this: there is no enabled rule that requires an alias to exist (AL01 only governs `AS` when one is present), and `uv run sqlfluff lint checks/order_line__composed_key.sql` reports "All Finished!". So the tool-is-the-rule exemption does not cover it, and it falls to review.

It is the only such reference in the repository. Grepping every committed `.sql` under `checks/`, `dar/uss/` and `docs/questions/*/` for a `FROM`/`JOIN` line without ` AS ` returns this line and nothing else — every other generated check aliases (`AS latest` in `order_details__key.sql:3`, `AS staged` in `order_details__clock.sql:3`, `AS b` in the five `measure__*__isolated.sql` files), and the outer query of this very file aliases its derived table `AS counted`.

The source is `src/adss/checks.py:341`, `f"    FROM {current.sql}\n"` inside `composed_key_checks`. Because the check is generated and committed with a `--check` regeneration gate, the fix belongs in the generator, not the file.
findings.why_it_matters: The convention exists so that generated and hand-written SQL are indistinguishable to a reviewer; a generator that emits an unaliased reference makes the committed artefact the counter-example the next author copies. It also lands in the file that is the whole point of ADR 0010 — the one check that proves the composed key does not collide.

findings.title: Business vocabulary in the machinery: "shipment" and "placement" in src/adss/checks.py
findings.detail:
The docstring of `measure_checks` reads: "By EVENT and not by stage. Two events on one entity share a stage, so a per-stage check would let **a parent's shipment measure sit on its placement row** and report nothing."

"shipment" and "placement" are the model's events `SHIPPED` and `PLACED` (`dab/uss.yaml:31` and `:8`) in noun form. conventions.md §5, hard rule: "**No data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code.** No entity, attribute or business term from the model appears in the machinery or in a test."

The provenance is visible: the same sentence in ADR 0012's Confirmation (line 143-144) reads "let **an order's** shipment measure sit on its placement row". The entity was neutralised to "a parent's" on the way into `src/`; the two event names were not. `grep -rniE 'shipment|placement|shipped|placed' src/ tests/ --include=*.py` returns this line and nothing else, so it is the single leak.

The neutral phrasing the file already uses elsewhere works here — "a measure of one event sit on another event's row".
findings.why_it_matters: §5's why is that the machinery must work for any source and any business model, and "a data name in it is proof that it does not". The comment is explaining a genuinely generic mechanism using this one business's events, which is exactly the leak the rule is aimed at, and the only one in the codebase.

findings.title: A blank line puts D-0002 outside the deviations register's table, so it does not render as an entry
findings.detail:
The register's table runs: header (line 17), delimiter (18), the D-0001 row (19). Line 20 is **blank**, and the D-0002 row is line 21.

In GitHub-flavoured Markdown a blank line terminates a table. D-0001 renders as the table's only row; line 21 renders as a paragraph of literal pipe-separated text with no columns, no header alignment, and no visible field labels — so the "Rule deviated from / Why / Cost / Exit condition / ADR / Status" structure that deviations.md's own "Entry format" section (lines 30-45) says every entry must have is invisible on the rendered page for the entry that has it.

conventions.md §8 covers the shape of these documents ("Prefer a table when there are three or more parallel things to say"; "except table rows, which stay on one line"), and this is the one document whose whole job is to make registered exceptions legible next to each other. Deleting line 20 fixes it.
findings.why_it_matters: The register is described as "read at the start of every slice" and its value is that entries can be scanned side by side against their exit conditions. A second entry that renders as a wall of pipes is the first step toward exactly what the document warns about: "a year later the rule is folklore." It is also the pattern the next deviation will be appended after.

result.summary:
Six conventions violations in slice 4, none of them caught by ruff/ty/sqlfluff/yamllint/pytest (all of which pass on this head).

The two that matter most are about where a definition and a rule are allowed to live. `das/contracts/order_details.yaml:48` puts business meaning in a DAS contract description — "This is the price on the line, which is not necessarily the product's current price" — which restates `dab/model.yaml:149-152`'s `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE`, breaking §1.1 ("Never what it means to the business") and §1.2 ("the only place the data is explained"). And ADR 0012 line 71 records that the new query-time rule "is written into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule": it was not — ADR 0002 line 112 still says "Two rules" — and under `docs/adr/README.md` it could not be, since only the Confirmation section may be edited. ADR 0012 contradicts itself on this at line 79.

The same rule is missing from conventions.md §10 while being stated in two SKILL.md files, which is the second-copy-with-no-first-copy drift the conventions preamble exists to prevent.

Then three smaller ones: the generated `checks/order_line__composed_key.sql:7` is the only unaliased table reference in any committed SQL (§3, and sqlfluff cannot see it); `src/adss/checks.py:374` leaks the model's event names ("shipment", "placement") into the machinery (§5); and a blank line at `docs/deviations.md:20` puts the new D-0002 entry outside the register's Markdown table.

Everything else checked out: the measure name `REVENUE_ORDER_LINES_AMOUNT` matches §2 exactly (it is conventions.md's own worked example), M1-M7 hold for `order-line-mapping.yaml` including the composed key and the relationship's target-expression shape, the ADR 0002 edit stayed inside the Confirmation exception, all four new ADRs landed before the code they decide, the question file references definitions rather than restating them, and the neutral test fixtures name nothing from the business.

findings.title: The inherited event date joins across two dlt load packages, and `das ingest` always lands `order_details` before `orders` — so on a clean lake every ORDER_LINE bridge row is dropped
findings.detail:
In `ordered__order_line_is_part_of_order` (dar/uss/_bridge.sql:117-143) the inherited date is resolved with:

    LEFT JOIN dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS dated
        ON pair."ORDER_key" = dated."ORDER_key"
        AND revision._observed_at >= dated.eff_tmstp

emitted by src/adss/uss.py:307 (`AND dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at`).

The two sides of that comparison come from *different sources*, and therefore from different clocks:
- `revision._observed_at` is `view_ORDER_LINE_hist.eff_tmstp` = `das__staged.order_details.extracted_at`
- `dated.eff_tmstp` is `view_ORDER_hist.eff_tmstp` = `das__staged.orders.extracted_at`

and `extracted_at` is `to_timestamp(cast(landed._dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))` (src/adss/das.py:71) — the dlt load id, which is per-`pipeline.run()`. `land()` creates one pipeline per contract (`pipeline_name=f"adss_das_{contract.table}"`, src/adss/landing.py:55) and `das_ingest` iterates `project.contract_paths()`, which is `tuple(sorted(...))` (src/adss/project.py:105), i.e. customers, **order_details, then orders** (src/adss/cli.py:133-137). So on every ingest, `extracted_at(order_details) < extracted_at(orders)`, strictly.

Measured, from the load ids in the parquet filenames of the last ingest on this machine:
  customers      1788841598.6610541
  order_details  1788841598.9334092
  orders         1788841599.2175243

A 0.28 s gap, in the wrong direction. For the only ORDER version that exists on a clean lake, `revision._observed_at (…598.933) >= dated.eff_tmstp (…599.218)` is FALSE. `dated` is NULL for every line, `_event_date` is NULL for every line, and the `ordered` CTE's `WHERE order_line_is_part_of_order._event_date IS NOT NULL` (dar/uss/_bridge.sql:156) removes all 2,155 rows. `dar__uss._bridge` gets zero `_stage = 'order_line'` rows, `uss.sql` returns 0 rows against `staged.sql`'s 23, and q04 fails.

The reason it is green here is an accident of this working tree's history: `das/lake/` is gitignored, and it happens to hold 12 `orders` loads *older* than the earliest `order_details` load (earliest order_details = 1788840845.976; 12 orders loads predate it, back to 1788819069). Under FULL_LOG those older ORDER versions are still in `view_ORDER_hist`, one of them satisfies the `<=`, and because the fixture never changes it carries the same `PLACED_ON`. Delete `das/lake/` (or clone fresh — .gitignore:28 ignores it and the note above it says "Everything in it is reproducible from das/fixtures via `uv run adss build --offline`") and the very first ingest has no such older version.

Nothing in the suite covers it. The new tests in tests/test_uss.py are text assertions over the generated SQL (`assert re.search(r"dated\.eff_tmstp\s*<=\s*revision\._observed_at", resolved)`), and the only test that runs the SQL against data, tests/test_fan_out.py, inserts a single constant `WHEN = "2026-01-01"` (tests/test_fan_out.py:37) into *both* `view_PARENT_hist.eff_tmstp` and `view_CHILD_hist.eff_tmstp`, so the parent is never observed later than the child that inherits from it. The generated data checks don't cover it either: `order_line_is_part_of_order__resolves.sql` counts *dangling* bridge rows and passes vacuously when there are none.

The fix is not the `<=` itself — ADR 0006/0009 are right that the parent must be resolved as of the child's observation. It is that a contract's `extracted_at` is a per-load clock, so "as of" comparisons across two contracts landed by the same `das ingest` are ordering-dependent. Either give one ingest one clock for all contracts, or make the inherited-date resolution fall back to the earliest parent version when none precedes the child.
findings.why_it_matters: The slice's headline result — 23 months, 1,265,793.0395 — is reproducible only on a lake that already contains an earlier `orders` load. On the clean rebuild the repository documents as the way to reproduce everything, the `ordered` branch of the bridge is empty and q04 does not build. It fails loudly rather than silently, which is good, but the committed, screenshotted, green slice does not build from a fresh clone.

findings.title: ADR 0009's Confirmation names a data check that the generator does not produce
findings.detail:
The Confirmation section ends: "A data check asserts that every bridge row's `_event_date` for such a stage equals the inherited entity's own date for the key on that row — the property that would break silently if the two were ever resolved at different instants."

No such check exists. `_generated_checks` (src/adss/cli.py:276-281) composes exactly `relationship_checks(model) | measure_checks(uss) | composed_key_checks(mappings, contracts)`, and `src/adss/checks.py` has no generator that mentions `_event_date` or the inherited date at all. `ls checks/` after this slice yields only the clock, key, measure-isolation, relationship (loaded / one_target / resolves) and composed-key checks — nothing that compares an inherited `_event_date` back to the parent's own date.

Since `adss dar generate --check` compares the committed `checks/` directory against what regenerates, and both are missing the check equally, nothing flags the discrepancy.
findings.why_it_matters: The ADR's own stated confirmation is the only thing standing behind the claim that an inherited date and its key are resolved at one instant. Written down as done and not built, it reads as covered to anyone auditing the decision — and it is the class of check that would have surfaced the inherited-date resolution problem above rather than leaving it to a stale lake to hide.

result.summary:
INDEPENDENT RECOMPUTATION: EXACT AGREEMENT.

I recomputed q04 from `das/fixtures/` alone using plain Python (json with `parse_float=Decimal`, collections, decimal) — no `src/adss` import, no warehouse read, no adss command, no reuse of the question's SQL. Revenue was derived from `dab/model.yaml`'s ORDER_LINE.REVENUE ("the quantity times the agreed price, less the discount on it") and the contract's typing in `das/contracts/order_details.yaml`, i.e. `Quantity * UnitPrice * (1 - Discount)` in exact decimal; the month came from the inherited `Orders.OrderDate` joined on `OrderId`.

Shape: 2,155 order lines (matching `@odata.count`), 2,155 distinct (OrderId, ProductId) pairs and 2,155 distinct `oid-pid` composed keys, 830 orders, no duplicates, no nulls in any of the five line fields, no line orphaned from an order, no order without a line, 1 to 25 lines per order, 838 lines discounted, and 23 distinct order months. All match the question's claims.

Per month, mine against the accepted screenshot's table (which is legible through 1997-10) — every visible row identical to the last digit:
  1996-07   27,861.8950  vs  27,861.8950  ✓
  1996-08   25,485.2750  vs  25,485.2750  ✓
  1996-09   26,381.4000  vs  26,381.4000  ✓
  … all 16 visible rows agree, including 1997-04 53,032.9525, 1997-09 55,629.2425 and 1997-10 66,749.2260 …
  1998-05   18,333.6305  (last month, below the screenshot's fold; the chart's faded bar and the "recording stops inside that month" caption match it)
Total: 1,265,793.0395 across 23 months from 2,155 lines — exactly the claimed figure. The page's derived statements check out too: best whole month 1998-04 at 123,798.6825 → "123,799"; recording ends 1998-05-06; 14 orders in 1998-05 against 74 in 1998-04.

ADR 0011's arithmetic claims also hold on the real values: max scale of any single revenue value is 4 (no line exceeds it), and no UnitPrice or Discount literal carries more than 4 places, so the DECIMAL(18,4) contract is lossless here.

ADR 0012's freight numbers all reproduce exactly, arithmetically from the fixtures:
  true freight over 830 orders                                   64,942.6900  ✓
  freight × lines-per-order (the `_event = 'ordered'` trap)      207,306.1000  ✓ (3.192×)
  freight × (placed + shipped) rows (the slice-3 shape)          128,897.7100  ✓ (1.985×)
  bridge rows 830 placed + 809 shipped + 2,155 ordered =              3,794  ✓

So: no disagreement anywhere between my numbers and the ones the slice publishes.

What I did find, while working out how the inherited date is actually resolved, is that the number is only reproducible on this machine's accumulated lake — the two findings below.

findings.title: ADR 0009's Confirmation claims a data check on the inherited event date that does not exist anywhere
findings.detail:
The Confirmation section ends: "A data check asserts that every bridge row's `_event_date` for such a stage equals the inherited entity's own date for the key on that row — the property that would break silently if the two were ever resolved at different instants."

No such check exists. `grep -rn "_event_date" checks/ src/adss/checks.py` returns nothing. The complete contents of `checks/` after this slice are: `customers__{clock,key}`, `orders__{clock,key}`, `order_details__{clock,key}`, `order_is_placed_by_customer__{one_target,loaded,resolves}`, `order_line_is_part_of_order__{one_target,loaded,resolves}`, `order_line__composed_key`, and five `measure__*__isolated` files. None of them reads `_event_date`, and no emitter in `src/adss/checks.py` produces one — the module has `relationship_checks`, `composed_key_checks` and `measure_checks` and nothing else.

The same paragraph (line 117) also claims tests/test_uss.py asserts the unreachable-date refusal happens "naming the available edges". `tests/test_uss.py:549-551` only does `pytest.raises(UssError, match="no edge")`; deleting the `f"{entity.id} reaches {sorted(reachable) or 'nothing'}. "` clause from `src/adss/uss.py:225` leaves that test green.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the ADR-claims-a-check-that-does-not-exist defect class the repository treats as serious. It is worse here than a documentation slip, because the property really is unprotected: on the real warehouse every entity has exactly one version per key (830 ORDER rows / 830 distinct keys, 2155 ORDER_LINE / 2155), so the q04 control-vs-answer comparison cannot distinguish "the order's date as of the line's observation" from "the order's date as of any other instant". A reader auditing D-0001 or ADR 0006's as-of rule will find the Confirmation and stop looking.

findings.title: No test ever executes the inherited-date bridge SQL, so two mutations of the slice's new date mechanism survive the whole suite
findings.detail:
`tests/test_fan_out.py` is the only test that builds a warehouse and runs generated bridge SQL, and `_build` reads `FIXTURES / "uss.yaml"` — the sidecar with no inherited-date event. The inherited-date sidecar `tests/fixtures/dab/inherited_date.yaml` is only ever passed to `read_uss` and checked with substring/regex matches over the emitted text (`tests/test_uss.py:511-568`). That is precisely what `tests/test_fan_out.py`'s own module docstring says is not good enough ("A substring assertion would pass a generator that emitted the right typed nulls in the wrong branch").

Two mutations I applied, ran, and reverted — `uv run pytest -q` stayed fully green (204 passed) for both:

(1) `src/adss/uss.py:331` — `",\n        dated.eff_tmstp DESC"` -> `",\n        dated.eff_tmstp ASC"`. This makes the walk pick the *oldest* version of the parent rather than the one in force at the inheriting row's observation instant. I built the neutral fixture with `inherited_date.yaml`, gave P1 two versions (HAPPENED_ON 2026-01-01 effective 2026-01-05, corrected to 2026-03-01 effective 2026-02-05) and a child observed 2026-06-01: correct code yields `_event_date = 2026-03-01`, the mutant yields `2026-01-01`. The regex at `tests/test_uss.py:527` only pins the join predicate `dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at`; nothing pins the ORDER BY direction.

(2) `src/adss/uss.py:302` — `dates = inherited == target.id` -> `dates = inherited is not None`. Every edge CTE then tries to select the inherited date column, so for an entity with more than one outbound edge the generator emits SQL DuckDB rejects (`Binder Error: Table "dated" does not have a column named "HAPPENED_ON"` — it reaches for it in the CHILD->NEIGHBOUR CTE). The neutral fixture has exactly that shape (CHILD has POINTS_AT and SITS_BESIDE), which is why the fixture exists; nothing builds it, so the suite passes.

Neither is caught by another gate either: `adss dar generate --check` only compares committed SQL against the generator (a developer who regenerates gets a green diff), and `adss check` cannot see (1) because the real data has one version per key.
findings.why_it_matters: The inherited event date is the mechanism this slice added, and it is the only new mechanism with no executable test. Mutation (1) silently dates a line by a stale version of its order — a wrong month in the finance analyst's chart, with every check and both acceptance queries green. Mutation (2) is the shape slice 5 walks into (an entity with a second edge), and it fails at build time with a message that points at the generator's output rather than its cause. Adding the inherited-date sidecar as a second parametrisation of `test_fan_out.py`'s `_build` would close both.

findings.title: The new formatter round-trip test covers key_check_sql but not composed_key_checks, the other emitter that counts distinct tuples
findings.detail:
`test_a_generated_check_still_runs_after_the_formatter_has_been_over_it` exists because sqlfluff strips the parentheses that make `count(DISTINCT (a, b))` a tuple. It only exercises `key_check_sql(contract)` (line 82). `composed_key_checks` — added in this same slice, and the only other emitter that builds `count(DISTINCT ROW(...))` (`src/adss/checks.py:339`) — is covered by neither this test nor `emitters()` (lines 28-44 list raw/staged/current/clock_check/key_check/bridge/peripheral/calendar/relationship_*/measure_*, no composed_key_*). `tests/test_composed_key_check.py` runs the emitter's raw output, never `formatted()`.

Mutation applied, run, reverted: `src/adss/checks.py:339`, `count(DISTINCT ROW({parts}))` -> `count(DISTINCT ({parts}))`. Full `uv run pytest -q`: green, 204 passed. `sqlfluff lint` on the resulting committed check: `All Finished!`, exit 0. But `formatted()` rewrites it to `count(DISTINCT order_id, product_id)`, and executing that gives `BinderException: No function matches the given name and argument types 'count(INTEGER, INTEGER)'`.
findings.why_it_matters: `run_checks` executes every file in `checks/` through `_zero` with no exception handling (`src/adss/checks.py:56,78`), so an unrunnable check raises out of `adss check` and aborts the run before a single finding is printed — the exact failure both the das.py comment and this test's docstring say they exist to prevent. The whole local gate (pytest + pre-commit: ruff, ty, sqlfluff, yamllint) stays green; only the CI `build and check` job fails, with a DuckDB binder error instead of a data finding.

findings.title: test_a_measure_is_checked_against_the_events_own_entity_not_the_one_it_inherits_from cannot fail for the reason it states
findings.detail:
The test's docstring describes the defect fixed in commit 9f96ca2 ("Resolving the date by reassigning the entity checked every measure against the wrong one"), but its only assertion is `assert any(e.id == "REACHED" for e in uss.events)` — it just checks `read_uss` returned the event.

The code path it names is never entered. `src/adss/uss.py:236` is guarded by `if measure.attribute_id and ...`, and the fixture's REACHED event (`tests/fixtures/dab/inherited_date.yaml`) declares only `{id: REACHED_CHILDREN_COUNT, aggregate: count}` — a count measure has `attribute_id = None`, so the loop body is skipped for every measure of the only event with an inherited date.

Mutation applied, run, reverted: `src/adss/uss.py:236`, `entity.attribute(...)` -> `dater.attribute(...)` (i.e. reverting 9f96ca2). `uv run pytest -q tests/test_uss.py tests/test_fan_out.py tests/test_measure_checks.py` -> all green. The full suite does catch it, but only via `tests/test_questions.py` reading the real `dab/uss.yaml`, and only as an unhandled `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute 'REVENUE'"` — i.e. because the production model happens not to have an attribute of that name on ORDER, not because the neutral fixture proves anything.

The converse half of the defect is untested anywhere: a sum measure naming an attribute the event's own entity does *not* have but the date-inherited entity *does* would be wrongly accepted, and nothing in `tests/` or `checks/` would notice.
findings.why_it_matters: Conventions §6 keeps the neutral fixture so machinery tests prove the machinery is generic rather than asserting it against this business's model. Here the guard for a bug that was actually shipped and fixed in this slice rests entirely on a coincidence of the production vocabulary. Giving REACHED a sum measure over `CHILD_WEIGHT` (an attribute PARENT does not have) would make the test fail for the reason it claims.

result.summary:
Four findings, all verified by applying a mutation, running `uv run pytest -q`, and reverting; the working tree is clean and the suite green (204 passed).

The serious one is an ADR Confirmation claiming a check that does not exist: ADR 0009 (line 123) says "A data check asserts that every bridge row's `_event_date` for such a stage equals the inherited entity's own date for the key on that row". No such check exists in `checks/` or in `src/adss/checks.py`, and the property is genuinely unprotected on the real warehouse (one version per key, so q04's control-vs-answer comparison cannot see it).

The largest test-quality gap is that nothing executes the inherited-date bridge SQL. `tests/test_fan_out.py` is the only test that builds and runs generated SQL, and it builds only `fixtures/dab/uss.yaml`; the inherited-date sidecar is checked with substring matches alone. Two mutations of the slice's new date mechanism — reversing the `dated.eff_tmstp DESC` tiebreak (wrong parent version, wrong month, silently) and widening the `dates` predicate to any inherited date (SQL DuckDB rejects for any entity with two edges) — leave the whole suite green.

`composed_key_checks` sits outside the new formatter round-trip test that was written for exactly its failure mode: emitting `count(DISTINCT (a, b))` instead of `count(DISTINCT ROW(a, b))` passes pytest and sqlfluff, but aborts `adss check` with a binder error before any finding prints.

And `test_a_measure_is_checked_against_the_events_own_entity_not_the_one_it_inherits_from` asserts only that the event exists — the fixture's inherited-date event has a `count` measure with no attribute, so the branch it names is never entered, and reverting the fix it was written for leaves `tests/test_uss.py` green.

The other slice-4 tests held up: `measure_checks` per-stage-instead-of-per-event is caught, the composed-key collision tests are caught, and the question-refusal tests behave as ADR 0012 describes.

findings.title: A fresh `adss build` silently produces an empty ORDER_LINE stage: the inherited-date join requires the PARENT to have been landed before the CHILD, and `das ingest` lands them the other way round
findings.detail:
`_inherit_cte` resolves the inherited date with `AND dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at` (uss.py:307, emitted as `AND revision._observed_at >= dated.eff_tmstp` at dar/uss/_bridge.sql:133). `revision._observed_at` is the CHILD entity's `eff_tmstp` and `dated.eff_tmstp` is the PARENT's. Both are `extracted_at` (mapping rule M4), and `extracted_at` is the per-contract dlt load-id timestamp (`to_timestamp(cast(landed._dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`, das.py:71). `das_ingest` (cli.py:132-137) calls `land()` once per contract in `project.contract_paths()` order, which is the sorted glob: customers.yaml, order_details.yaml, orders.yaml. So within one build ORDER_LINE.eff_tmstp is strictly EARLIER than ORDER.eff_tmstp, the join matches nothing, `_event_date` is null on every line, and the stage's own `WHERE order_line_is_part_of_order._event_date IS NOT NULL` (uss.py:374, _bridge.sql:156) removes all 2,155 rows.

Reproduced end to end. I exported the branch tip with `git archive` into a scratch directory (no lake, no warehouse, no .dlt — i.e. a clean checkout) and ran `adss build`. It reported success for every step. The resulting warehouse:

  bridge by event: [('placed', 830), ('shipped', 809)]        <- no 'ordered' at all
  ORDER hist eff:      2026-09-08 05:19:50.849661
  ORDER_LINE hist eff: 2026-09-08 05:19:50.529184
  order_line peripheral rows: 2155
  sum(_measure__order_line__revenue_order_lines_amount): None

`adss check` on that warehouse: all 40 generated data checks PASS (including `measure__order_line__revenue_order_lines_amount__isolated` and `order_line_is_part_of_order__resolves`, both of which pass vacuously on an empty stage), q01-q03 pass, and the single failure is `FAIL q04: the source and the star schema agree — 23 control rows, 0 answer rows`. `pytest` also passes 204/204 against that build.

The committed `warehouse.duckdb` only works by accident of history: ORDER was first landed at 2026-09-07 22:11:09.111026 — before order_details existed as a contract — and DAB's FULL_LOG keeps the original `eff_tmstp` for unchanged rows, so `view_ORDER_hist` still carries that one old timestamp while `view_ORDER_LINE_hist` carries 2026-09-08 04:14. Rename `orders.yaml` to anything sorting before `order_details.yaml`, drop the warehouse and lake, or add a second finer-grained entity whose parent sorts later, and the stage vanishes again.
findings.why_it_matters: Blueprint S2 promises DAB and DAR are rebuildable from DAS at any time. They are not: the slice's headline deliverable — 2,155 line rows and 1,265,793.0395 of revenue — cannot be reproduced from a clean checkout, and the loss is silent everywhere except one question comparison. Nothing in ADR 0009, docs/deviations.md or the question documents mentions load ordering; ADR 0009 only anticipates 'a line whose order cannot be resolved', which is not what is happening here (the pair resolves fine; it is the parent's history row that is out of reach). A production build that re-ingests both contracts in the normal order would ship a page whose whole answer is empty.

findings.title: The parent version used for an inherited date is not required to be a dated one, so a child row can disappear while its parent's own event stays dated
findings.detail:
For an event's OWN date, `_version_cte` filters `WHERE revision.<date> IS NOT NULL` (uss.py:268) BEFORE the `QUALIFY row_number() ... ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC = 1`, which is what makes the docstring's 'the latest version in which it is dated' (uss.py:244) true. The inherited path does not do this: the `dated` join (uss.py:304-310) has no null filter, and the ranking tiebreak is a bare `dated.eff_tmstp DESC` (uss.py:331). So it picks the parent's latest version at or before the child's observation time, dated or not, and the stage's `WHERE ... _event_date IS NOT NULL` then deletes the child row.

Reproduced against `tests/fixtures/dab/inherited_date.yaml`: PARENT P1 with two history rows — eff 2026-01-01 with HAPPENED_ON = 2025-06-01, and a later eff 2026-01-02 with HAPPENED_ON = NULL — and one CHILD C1 observed 2026-01-03 pointing at P1. The generated bridge returns:

  happened rows (parent's own event): [('happened', date(2025, 6, 1))]
  reached rows (child, inherited):    []

Same entity, same attribute, two different answers, no error. The fix is symmetry: the parent's date has to be non-null for the version to be a candidate (add it to the join predicate, or rank `dated.<date> IS NOT NULL DESC, dated.eff_tmstp DESC`), not filtered after the winner is picked.
findings.why_it_matters: A source that blanks a date on a correction — a common shape in FULL_LOG history — makes a whole grain's rows vanish from the bridge while the coarser grain's rows for the same entity stay put. Two answers over one warehouse then disagree about how many things happened, and the generated checks cannot see it: the measure-isolation check counts leaks only, and the relationship `__resolves` check only inspects rows that reached the bridge.

findings.title: The aggregate refusal rejects every zero-argument window function (`row_number`, `rank`, `ntile`, ...) with the count(*) message, which is neither true nor actionable
findings.detail:
`_aggregate_names()` (question.py:87-99) takes every name `duckdb_functions()` types as `aggregate`. I checked what that set actually contains: `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist`, `ntile`, `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `nth_value` are all in it. `aggregated()` then reports a zero-argument window call with an empty column tuple, and the `if not columns` branch (question.py:159-163) raises:

  "the answer query says row_number() over no column, which counts measurement events rather than the thing anybody asked about -- two events on one entity and it doubles. Sum the measure that counts them instead."

Measured: the shipped q04 query is accepted; `sum(...) - lag(sum(...)) OVER (...)` over a measure column is correctly accepted; but

  SELECT cal.month_label, sum(b._measure__order_line__revenue_order_lines_amount),
         row_number() OVER (ORDER BY sum(b._measure__order_line__revenue_order_lines_amount) DESC) AS rk
  FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

is REFUSED. Every aggregate in it is over a protected measure column; the rank cannot multiply anything; and the advice given ('sum the measure that counts them instead') has nothing to do with `row_number()`. The docstring at question.py:118-121 states the assumption that is wrong: 'An aggregate with no columns at all -- count(*) -- comes back with none'. count(*) is not the only member of that set. The two strictnesses the docstring does document (count(*), and an aggregate over a DISTINCT peripheral column) are deliberate; this one is not, and is not written down anywhere.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Rank the months' / 'top N' is an ordinary shape for an answer query, and the next question that needs one is blocked by a refusal whose stated reason sends the author looking for a fan-out that is not there. Discriminating on `class == "WINDOW"` with an empty child list, or on the actual `count`/`count_star` names, separates the case the rule is about from the case it is not.

findings.title: ADR 0009's Confirmation section claims a data check that does not exist
findings.detail:
The record ends: 'A data check asserts that every bridge row's `_event_date` for such a stage equals the inherited entity's own date for the key on that row — the property that would break silently if the two were ever resolved at different instants.' No such check exists. `checks/` holds only the contract clock/key checks, the three relationship checks per edge, five `measure__*__isolated.sql` files and `order_line__composed_key.sql`; `src/adss/checks.py` generates `relationship_checks`, `measure_checks` and `composed_key_checks` and nothing that compares an inherited `_event_date` to a parent's attribute. This slice's own skills commit (ca3f329) adds the rule 'run the mutation before the ADR's Confirmation claims one — a confirmation naming a test that could not fail for the reason given is worse than no confirmation'; this is the same defect one step further along, a confirmation naming a check that does not exist at all.

Worth noting for the fix: had this check existed as described it would still have passed vacuously on the fresh build in finding 1, because there are no bridge rows for that stage to compare. A check that would have caught it has to compare the stage's row COUNT against the source, not just the dates of rows that survived.
findings.why_it_matters: The register and the ADRs are what a reader trusts instead of re-deriving the property. A Confirmation that names a non-existent check stops the next person looking — and the property it claims to guard is exactly the one that is broken on a fresh build.

findings.title: The revenue page marks the last month partial by position, and crashes when the answer has one row or none
findings.detail:
`a4.with_columns((pl.col("order_month") != a4["order_month"].max()).alias("complete"))` (app.py:536) does not derive whether the last month is partial — it asserts that the last month is always partial. If the recording ever ends on a month boundary the page still fades the final bar and captions it 'the recording stops inside that month' (app.py:~600), which is the page stating a fact it has not established; the commit message for this cell says that is the one thing the layer must not do.

The next line is a hard failure rather than a wrong caption: `best = (a4.filter(pl.col("complete")).sort(...)).row(0, named=True)` (app.py:539). When the answer has exactly one row, `complete` is False on it, the filter is empty and `.row(0)` raises. When the answer is empty — which is what a fresh build produces, per finding 1 — `a4["order_month"].max()` is None, the comparison is null, the filter is empty, and the page raises there instead of rendering. Guard the filter and fall back to the whole frame (or to a 'no whole month yet' headline).
findings.why_it_matters: The screenshot in docs/questions/04-revenue-per-order-month/answer.png is what the slice is accepted on, and the cell that produces it has no defined behaviour for a one-month or empty answer. Combined with finding 1 it means the acceptance artefact cannot be regenerated from a clean build at all — the page errors rather than showing an empty chart that would have made the loss obvious.

result.summary: Five verified defects, all reproduced rather than argued. The serious one is in the new inherited-date CTE: a fresh `adss build` from a clean checkout produces a bridge with 830 `placed` + 809 `shipped` rows and ZERO `ordered` rows — the whole ORDER_LINE grain, the entire point of slice 4, silently absent, with all 40 generated checks passing and only `q04: the source and the star schema agree` failing. The cause is that `dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at` (uss.py:307) requires the parent entity to have been landed no later than the child, while `das ingest` lands contracts in sorted filename order, putting order_details before orders. The committed warehouse works only because ORDER was first landed a day before ORDER_LINE existed. Second, the same join picks the parent's latest version whether or not it is dated, unlike the event's own date, so a null on a parent's latest revision deletes the child row while the parent's own event stays dated. Third, `question.py`'s new refusal treats every zero-argument window function (`row_number`, `rank`, `ntile`, ...) as `count(*)`, wrongly refusing a legitimate 'rank the months' answer query with an unrelated reason. Fourth, ADR 0009's Confirmation names a data check that does not exist. Fifth, the new destination cell asserts (rather than derives) that the last month is partial and raises on a one-row or empty answer. I found nothing wrong with the `ROW()` change in das.py, the composed-key check, the measure-isolation checks, or the two commands' sweeps over `checks/` — a full fresh build regenerated every committed file byte-identically and deleted nothing.\n\nMethod note: while I was reading, `src/adss/uss.py` and then `src/adss/checks.py` were being edited in the working tree by something else (single-line mutations — `dated.eff_tmstp DESC` to `ASC`, and `ROW(...)` back to bare parentheses), so I reviewed a clean `git archive` export of the branch tip at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad/tip rather than the checkout. The fresh build and all reproductions were run there; the real repository was only read from.

findings.title: D-0002's Cost and ADR 0011's Consequences claim an over-scale value is "refused"; DuckDB silently rounds it

The new deviation's Cost field reads: "A source value with more than the declared scale is refused rather than approximated, which is the right failure and still a failure somebody must handle". ADR 0011 line 111 says the same: "Bad, because a source value with more than four decimal places would now be refused rather than approximated.     CAST('0.12345' AS DECIMAL(18,4))  ->  0.1235      -- rounded, no error
    CAST('0.99999' AS DECIMAL(18,4))  ->  1.0000      -- rounded, no error

Today no discount in the recording exceeds two decimal places (I scanned all 22 fixture pages: the distinct values are 0, 0.01…0.06, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25), so nothing is currently being rounded. The claim is about behaviour, and the behaviour is wrong.
